articles.body: GEODIS is expanding its electric vehicle operations in Australia with the addition of a Volvo FM Electric Prime Mover. The new truck will support container transportation between Sydney’s Port Botany and Volvo’s local warehouse. The vehicle marks GEODIS’ entry into electric-powered container haulage in Australia. It also becomes the third electric truck in the company’s Australian fleet. The Volvo FM Electric will primarily transport full container loads carrying Volvo cargo from Port Botany to the manufacturer’s warehouse. GEODIS expects the truck to complete approximately 850 trips annually on this route. These operations will account for around 63% of the vehicle’s available capacity. Meanwhile, GEODIS will use the remaining capacity to support its new warehouse in Minto, located next to Volvo’s facility. Expanding electric container transport in Sydney The introduction of the electric prime mover extends GEODIS’ use of battery-powered vehicles into heavier-duty logistics operations. The Volvo FM Electric is designed to handle container haulage requirements while producing zero tailpipe emissions. In addition, its lower noise levels could offer benefits for transport operations across Sydney’s metropolitan area. The truck will also support GEODIS’ retail and e-commerce logistics activities through its Minto warehouse. The deployment adds a port-related application to GEODIS’ existing electric fleet operations in Australia, combining container transport with warehouse distribution services.

articles.body: Everllence has appointed Dr Fabian Kley as Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and member of its Executive Board, effective 1 November 2026. Kley has already led the company’s Finance division since March 2026. He will now formally assume the CFO position following a decision by the Everllence Supervisory Board. He joined Everllence in 2019 and has held several senior positions within the company. Most recently, he served as Senior Vice President, overseeing Corporate Strategy and Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A). During his time as Finance Director, Kley supported preparations for the company’s change in ownership to Bain Capital. He also worked on modernising financial reporting and management systems. Hauke Stars, Chairwoman of the Supervisory Board of Everllence, highlighted Kley’s contribution during the ownership transition. She also noted his role in preparing the finance organisation for the requirements of the new ownership structure. Meanwhile, Everllence CEO Uwe Lauber said Kley had contributed to the company’s strategic development and played an important operational role in the ownership transition. Before joining Everllence, Kley worked at consulting firm Booz & Company and energy technology company Schlumberger. He holds a doctorate in energy economics from the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and an MBA from the University of North Carolina. The appointment follows previous changes to Everllence’s financial leadership , which Container News reported in June 2025.

The Marshall Islands-flagged vessel was sailing toward the waterway loaded with LNG from Qatar when it came under fire, the people said, asking not to be named as they are not authorized to speak to the media. Just hours earlier, Iranian authorities were understood to have provided a green light, they added. The ship subsequently turned around and headed into the Persian Gulf, according to ship-tracking data. “Qatar reserves its right to take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law and the UN Charter, to protect its assets and safeguard its vessels and their crews,” the Qatari Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Sunday, adding that authorities are investigating the incident and those responsible. Pakistan , apparently benefiting from its ties with Iran and its role as mediator, has communicated with Iranian authorities over the safety of several other shipments of Qatari LNG over the past month, all of which crossed successfully into the Gulf of Oman. The incident underscores the continued risk for vessels navigating around Hormuz and poses a fresh challenge for Pakistan, which has grappled for months with an energy shortfall as a result of upheaval in the Middle East. Without the LNG shipment, Pakistan could be forced to turn to the spot market, where prices are more than three times pre-war levels. articles.title: Port Houston advances Project 12 planning
articles.summary: The Port Commission of the Port of Houston Authority convened its regular monthly meeting, with discussions spanning the recently completed Project 11 channel improvements, early planning for a potential Project 12 expansion and progress on the proposed Barbours Cut North Expansion Project. articles.body: The Port Commission of the Port of Houston Authority convened its regular monthly meeting, with discussions spanning the recently completed Project 11 channel improvements, early planning for a potential Project 12 expansion and progress on the proposed Barbours Cut North Expansion Project. Chairman Ric Campo reflected on the October celebration marking completion of the Port-led Project 11 segments and emphasised the continuing responsibility to invest in the Houston Ship Channel’s future as an extraordinary economic engine supporting jobs and prosperity for generations. Campo also highlighted the upcoming Houston International Maritime Conference from November 2 to 5, which will bring Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta and other industry experts to Houston, describing the participation of the leader of one of the world’s most important waterways as a significant opportunity to strengthen relationships and discuss the future of global maritime trade. CEO Charlie Jenkins announced that Port Houston will move forward with its own study for portions of a potential Project 12 under Section 203 of the Water Resources Development Act of 1986, running in parallel with the port’s partnership with the US Army Corps of Engineers on a traditional feasibility study for broader Houston Ship Channel and Galveston Bay system improvements. Earlier in the week, Port Houston and the Army Corps held a Federal Interest Determination meeting, initiating a 45-day process that will result in a recommendation on the Project 12 scope of study. On container capacity, the Army Corps held a public scoping meeting for a potential expansion north of Barbours Cut Terminal onto Spilman Island as Port Houston continues to evaluate options to accommodate the additional container capacity projected to be needed in the region over the next decade. Port Houston also hosted Permitting Council Executive Director Emily Domenech for a site tour to provide firsthand context for the early-stage planning process.

articles.body: LR Tankers: Freight Squeezes Naphtha Arb in Hellenic Shipping News 02/11/2026 A shift has been underway in the naphtha market as a result of the war in the Middle East. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “the war in the Middle East has upended Asia’s naphtha market. With the Gulf normally supplying over half of Asia’s imports, the March halt at Hormuz forced buyers to pay up for Western barrels. The wide East-West spread had kept Western naphtha flowing East, accounting for around 70% of Asia’s naphtha import volume. Yet Western loadings fell to 0.9 mt in October, their lowest this year and only about 20% of supply. Freight is the reason: moving a cargo from the Med to Japan now costs more than double what the spread pays. Asia has instead turned back East. Eastern loadings recovered to 3.9 mt in October, led by 2.9 mt from the Gulf of Oman via STS transfers, while ports inside Hormuz shipped just 90 kt directly. It is a sharp reversal from March, when Hormuz closed and the West briefly supplied close to 70% of Asia’s naphtha”. According to Gibson, “the spread itself is not the problem. It averaged about $65/mt in October, swinging between $45/mt and $120/mt, well above the $20-45/mt range that held through most of 2025. In March, it sat comfortably above the cost of moving naphtha from the Med to Japan, and Western barrels flowed. Since then, freight has risen far faster than the spread. LR2 Med/Japan freight has eased by around a quarter from its mid-October peak, but still sits well above the spread on a per-tonne basis. The arbitrage is technically shut, but cargoes are still moving, albeit in smaller volumes and increasingly on smaller ships”. “The ships tell the same story. LR2s lifted only 2 of October’s 24 Western cargoes, down from 6 in January, while MR cargoes doubled from 10 to 21. The shift is centred on the Med, which shipped 15 MR cargoes to Asia in October against just one in January, while the US Gulf sent only two. LR2 availability has been limited by heavy dirty-up activity since the war began. More LR2s are also positioned in the East than the West, with most engaged on westbound clean runs from the Middle East and India. Eastern naphtha has increasingly relied on LR1s and MRs. MRs lifted 22 Middle East naphtha cargoes in October, up from 15 in January, while LR2 cargoes fell to 10 from 31. Shorter-haul Eastern supply has not brought cheaper freight. LR1 and LR2 rates from the AG to Japan have more than doubled since July, and LR1 and MR rates from West Coast India to Japan have more than doubled since August. Tanker attacks, Gulf of Oman congestion and tight LR lists have kept every route into Asia firm, although AG LR rates eased slightly in the final week of October”, Gibson noted. Feedstock economics have improved, though cracker margins remain thin. The ethylene-naphtha spread fell back in October to below its 2025 average, as ethylene failed to keep pace with rising naphtha prices. Benzene and PX spreads sit close to breakeven. The propane-naphtha spread averaged around -$160/mt in April, when propane offered crackers a much cheaper feed. It has since narrowed to near zero, with both products trading around $1,040/mt in late October, removing much of the incentive to switch away from naphtha and restoring its competitiveness as a cracker feedstock in Asia. Weak downstream petrochemical margins and ongoing cracker rationalisation remain a cap on how far demand can recover. With the East-West spread well above 2025 levels but still short of freight, LR rates have become the bigger moving part: a $100/t swing in Med/Japan LR2 freight within October far outweighed the change in the spread, whose monthly average rose only around $12/mt. If LR freight continues to soften and moves closer to the spread, more Western naphtha could return on December loadings. Until then, Asia’s naphtha will come mainly from the Gulf of Oman and India, with freight costs driven largely by the LR market. articles.summary: Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US were mixed this week as capacity on the trade lane is expected to tighten slightly and import demand is expected to ease. Rates to the West Coast are between $7,515-8,365/FEU (40-foot equivalent unit) while rates to the East Coast are between...
articles.body: Asia-US container rates mixed as capacity tightens, import demand slows; tanker rates mostly higher in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US were mixed this week as capacity on the trade lane is expected to tighten slightly and import demand is expected to ease. Rates to the West Coast are between $7,515-8,365/FEU (40-foot equivalent unit) while rates to the East Coast are between $9,600-11,500/FEU, remaining near the highest since mid-2022 for both routes. Rates from supply chain advisors Drewry were lower, falling by 6% from Shanghai to Los Angeles and by 5% from Shanghai to New York, as shown in the following graph. Drewry said six blank sailings have been announced for next week, up from five this week, indicating tight capacity. Meanwhile, strong US import demand is easing, which could put further downward pressure on freight rates. Hence, Drewry expects rates to decrease next week. Rates from global logistics company Freight Right fell by 1% to the West Coast and rose by 0.22% to the East Coast, as shown in the following graph. Robert Khachatryan, founder and CEO of Freight Right, said that space is improving, with softer volumes and more consistent vessel schedules giving importers greater booking flexibility. “As the traditional pre-holiday ocean shipping peak fully closes out, pricing has settled into a steady holding pattern across both coasts,” Khachatryan said. Looking forward, Khachatryan expects China-US ocean rates to remain broadly stable through the first half of November, with the possibility of modest declines. Weekly rates from online shipping marketplace and platform provider Freightos rose by 3% to the West Coast and by 9% to the East Coast. Judah Levine, head of research at Freightos, said this week’s increases were a surprise as he expected transpacific prices would cool post-Golden Week. “Daily prices to the East Coast have receded so far this week but are still up about $200/FEU compared to last week,” Levine said. “Some forwarders, however, report signs of cooling demand and space becoming more available and still expect a seasonal easing in rates.” Rates on the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI), which tracks rates for containers leaving Shanghai, edged higher by 0.16%, rising for the fourth week in a row. Rates on the NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) rose by 1.9% to both coasts. Container ships and costs for shipping containers are relevant to the chemical industry because while most chemicals are liquids and are shipped in tankers, container ships transport polymers, such as polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), which are shipped in pellets. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is also shipped in containers. They also transport liquid chemicals in isotanks. LIQUID TANKER RATES MOSTLY HIGHER US chemical tanker freight rates assessed by ICIS were mostly higher this week along most major trade lanes, with increases for parcels from the US Gulf (USG) to Europe, Brazil, and India, with smaller changes along the Asia trade lane. For the USG to Rotterdam, there are limited bits of cargo space still available for November for small parcels. A lack of interest has prompted clean petroleum products (CPP) tonnage to focus on higher rates in the clean market, leaving limited availability for chemicals. It has been difficult for owners to accommodate larger parcels which has prompted rates to increase for those size cargoes. However, there seems to be more interest in caustic soda from USG to ARA, with at least one cargo of 10,000 tonnes for various November dates, as well as two 15,000-tonne cargoes of styrene, along with a large parcel of MEG (monoethylene glycol) all being fixed. Rates from the USG to Asia remained steady both for smaller parcels and for larger parcels. Overall, this trade lane remains dependent upon contract of affreightment (COA) volumes. Most players remain hesitant to take the opportunity due to the risk and uncertainty. Most cargoes discussed in the market were methanol, MEG, and ethylene dichloride (EDC) to southeast Asia. From the USG to Brazil, the market has been a bit more active this week particularly for smaller parcels. Overall, spot chemical trade on this route is relatively steady, however a tighter positions list supports the freight rates. Despite the uptick in inquiries there is not enough significant activity that would suggest any increase in demand. Most of the regular owners have space remaining and are trying to fill space while supporting current freight levels. COA volumes remain steady as there were some inquiries for caustic soda, MEG, and styrene moving to Brazil. Freight rates are now expected to remain pressured higher for the time being. Along the USG to India route, demand to WC India for MEG, methanol, and ethanol continue to prevail as several large parcels are looking for any available space. For the time being rates are slightly higher week on week. articles.body: Dry Bulk Shipping: Capesize Market Rebounding in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 02/11/2026 C apesize The market gathered momentum through the week, with improving sentiment and stronger fixing activity across both basins driving a broad-based recovery. The Pacific initially remained relatively subdued, with C5 fixtures holding around the high $13s to $14 as miners maintained a measured approach. However, increased competition for tonnage saw rates push through the $14 mark midweek, eventually reaching the low $15s by Thursday, reflecting a noticeably stronger market. Towards the close, the Pacific eased slightly, with activity becoming particularly limited and talk emerging of offers slipping back below the $15 mark. The Atlantic followed a similar trajectory, with the South Brazil and West Africa to China markets gaining considerable traction as fixing activity intensified. C3 rates advanced from the mid-$34s to the high $36s, supported by a gradually tightening ballaster list. With most end-November cargoes covered, attention has increasingly shifted towards December dates. North Atlantic sentiment also improved, supported by stronger Fronthaul fixtures and fresh enquiry. Overall, sentiment improved considerably, with the BCI 182 5TC climbing from $33,795 on Monday to $37,420 by Friday, with gains across all major routes and a more positive outlook heading into the coming week. Panamax-Kamsarmax The Atlantic remained the weaker basin throughout the week, with limited cargo enquiry and a growing tonnage count keeping sentiment firmly in charterers’ favour. Transatlantic demand remained thin, while subdued grain and mineral activity provided little support to rates. An 82,000-dwt fixed a transatlantic grains round trip at $17,500, while a 79,000-dwt fixed basis delivery East Coast South America for an Atlantic trip at $25,000. Fronthaul conditions were similarly pressured, particularly from EC South America, as continued ballasting from the Indian Ocean added to tonnage availability. However, improving demand towards the end of the week offered some encouragement, with an 82,000-dwt fixing retroactively from East Coast India in mid-October at $17,000 and a 75,000-dwt fixing basis delivery East Coast South America at $18,000 plus an $800,000 ballast bonus. The Pacific also softened, with limited North Pacific activity and reduced EC Australian requirements weighing on sentiment. An 82,000-dwt and an 84,000-dwt both fixed North Pacific round trips at $20,000, while a 75,000-dwt fixed an East Coast Australia round trip at $17,000. Indonesian demand provided some stability but remained insufficient to offset wider pressure, with a 77,000-dwt fixing a shorter Indonesia to South China trip at $17,000. Overall, owners faced increasing competition for employment, with the P5TC declining steadily throughout the week as rates remained under sustained pressure. Ultramax/Supramax The Atlantic was negative this week, with rates dropping in the US Gulf as grains and petcoke stems became scarce. A 64,000-dwt fixed a wood pellets stem to the UK at $31,000 and a similar type was fixed with petcoke via Panama Canal to China at $31,250, but another 63,000-dwt fixed a grains stem to China via Cape of Good Hope at $28,500, which was apparently the only direction the vessel was able to consider. Further south, the market was under pressure from the larger Panamax vessels with a 63,000-dwt fixed from Recalada to the East at $19,750 plus $975,000 ballast bonus at the beginning of the week, and a Japanese built 61,000-dwt reported fixed to Southeast Asia at $18,250 plus $825,000 ballast bonus later in the week. Rates on the Continent are still good, but the highs for scrap cargoes have passed with rates now said to be low $30,000’s, and the East Mediterranean was more active than the West. Asia remained firm amid lighter trading with the North still the driving force with a 63,000-dwt ex dry dock China fixed to West Africa with generals at $28,000, whilst the South Pacific was more subdued this week. The Indian Ocean was also quieter, and rates softened with a 61,000-dwt fixed basis Kandla for a trip Chittagong at $16,000 with aggregates. Period activity again centred in the firmer areas with a 63,000-dwt open South China fixed for minimum 3 to about 6 months at $24,000, with first employment a trip to the Maldives. Handysize The market was subdued all week, and the HS7TC average finished the week slightly below last week’s close, amid positional trading. EC South America remained the firmest area of the Atlantic, but rates seemed to plateau amid slow trading, whilst the US Gulf dropped in the second half of the week with sources saying trips Skaw-Passero were now bid in the mid-teens, whilst a nice 40,000-dwt fixed basis SW Pass for a trip Atlantic Colombia at $16,000. The Continent remained firm due to a shortage of tonnage nearby, but the Mediterranean suffered due to a lack of fresh enquiry. There was limited news from the Pacific, however, the North was well supported and rates nudged up during the week, with a 39,000-dwt open South Korea fixed to West Coast Central America at $19,000. Period activity became positional in uncertain conditions, with a 37,000-dwt open Paranaguá fixed 5 to 7 months redelivery within the Atlantic at $20,800. articles.title: Can carriers avoid overcapacity in 2027?
articles.summary: Earlier this week, Drewry hosted one of its regular webinars examining the outlook for the container shipping market and the forces shaping the supply-demand balance in 2027. We also polled attendees on two questions: how they expect the market to evolve next year, and which factors will ultimately determine whether...
articles.body: Can carriers avoid overcapacity in 2027? in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 E arlier this week, Drewry hosted one of its regular webinars examining the outlook for the container shipping market and the forces shaping the supply-demand balance in 2027. We also polled attendees on two questions: how they expect the market to evolve next year, and which factors will ultimately determine whether it tips into overcapacity. The backdrop is difficult to ignore. Around 5 mteu of new capacity has been ordered in each of the past three years, pushing the orderbook-to-fleet ratio to approximately 45%, its highest level since 2009. The orderbook is fast approaching 16 mteu, with September the second-busiest contracting month on record at 1.1 mteu, following major orders from the world’s two largest carriers: MSC (20 × 24,000 teu) and Maersk (20 × 18,600 teu). The counterargument is that traditional supply-demand fundamentals no longer tell the whole story. Geopolitical disruption, port congestion and longer sailing distances have become increasingly influential, absorbing capacity and limiting the amount of nominal fleet capacity available to carry cargo. Ultimately, the 2027 outcome will depend on whether demand growth, slow steaming and congestion can absorb capacity faster than new ships enter service. Our view? They won’t. These disruptive forces are now structurally embedded in the market and will undoubtedly slow the conversion of nominal capacity into effective supply. But the sheer volume of new tonnage arriving means their ability to offset fleet growth will diminish. Overcapacity is, in our view, unavoidable. Its severity is the real uncertainty. The verdict from our poll Our webinar attendees broadly agreed. More than 70% expect some degree of overcapacity in 2027, with 56.7% anticipating a moderate surplus and 14.2% predicting significant overcapacity. Just 14.4% expect the market to remain broadly balanced, while only 5.3% foresee a tight market. The consensus is clear: industry participants recognise the structural pressure from fleet expansion, even if they disagree on how severe the resulting imbalance will be. What could tip the balance? Newbuild deliveries were identified as the biggest determining factor by 39.4% of respondents, reinforcing the scale of concern over incoming capacity. However, 29.0% pointed to network disruption and port congestion, highlighting the continuing importance of effective rather than nominal supply. Longer voyages, schedule unreliability and ships waiting outside congested ports can all absorb capacity that would otherwise be available to carry cargo. Carrier capacity management ranked third, at 18.6%. Blank sailings, service adjustments and other measures can help contain the surplus, but respondents appear unconvinced that carriers can fully offset the delivery pipeline. Cargo demand attracted just 11.7%, while demolitions accounted for only 1.3%, suggesting that neither stronger demand nor the removal of older tonnage is widely expected to be the decisive factor. Our view The poll reinforces our assessment that 2027 will be a test of carriers’ ability to manage a growing capacity surplus rather than prevent one altogether. If congestion eases and more vessels return to productive service just as deliveries accelerate, pressure on utilisation, freight rates and earnings could intensify. Persistent disruption and disciplined capacity management could soften the impact, but relying on inefficiencies to keep the market balanced is a precarious strategy. Source: Drewry Tops 2026-11-02 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 E arlier this week, Drewry hosted one of its regular webinars examining the outlook for the container shipping market and the forces shaping the supply-demand balance in 2027.
We also polled attendees on two questions: how they expect the market to evolve next year, and which factors will ultimately determine whether it tips into overcapacity.
The backdrop is difficult to ignore.

articles.summary: The US Trade Representative (USTR) will take public comment through 30 October and is suspending the implementation of port fees for Chinese vessels by two months as officials from both countries continue to negotiate broader trade issues. The new fees were set to take effect on 10 November after the US and China...
articles.body: US suspends Chinese vessel port fees for 2 months, will accept public comment in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 The US Trade Representative (USTR) will take public comment through 30 October and is suspending the implementation of port fees for Chinese vessels by two months as officials from both countries continue to negotiate broader trade issues. The new fees were set to take effect on 10 November after the US and China agreed in November 2025 to suspend tit-for-tat maritime charges for one year as part of a broader trade agreement. They will now take effect on 9 January if no other agreement is reached. The temporary suspension means that no parties will accrue liability for, or be required to pay, the transport service fees or associated product duties during the extended window. The US initially targeted the fees for ships owned, operated, or built in China in October 2025, prompting China to enact similar charges for US-linked ships entering Chinese ports. The initial USTR proposal was published in February 2025 in the Federal Register and included proposed service fees of up to $1.5 million per US port call for vessels built in China, and up to $1 million per port call for China-based operators. The action was taken after a Section 301 investigation determined China’s acts, policies and practices to be unreasonable and to burden or restrict US commerce. Section 301 is a provision of the Trade Act of 1974 that allows the US to investigate and act against trade practices by foreign companies that are deemed unfair. Brokers in the liquid bulk market are continuing to monitor the situation and are taking a wait-and-see approach before making any hard decisions. Most liquid tankers are built in China, Japan and South Korea. Action taken against container ships could also impact chemicals markets because while most chemicals are liquids and are shipped in tankers, container ships transport polymers, such as polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), are shipped in pellets. They also transport liquid chemicals in isotanks. articles.title: LNG Carrier Prices Fall to $245 Million, Threatening Korean Shipbuilders’ Margins
articles.summary: Prices for high-value vessels, including liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers and ultra-large container ships, have begun to decline despite rising demand. Intensifying competition from Chinese shipbuilders entering the premium vessel market, coupled with their aggressive supply strategies, is putting downward...
articles.body: LNG Carrier Prices Fall to $245 Million, Threatening Korean Shipbuilders’ Margins in Shipbuilding News 02/11/2026 Prices for high-value vessels, including liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers and ultra-large container ships, have begun to decline despite rising demand. Intensifying competition from Chinese shipbuilders entering the premium vessel market, coupled with their aggressive supply strategies, is putting downward pressure on newbuilding prices. According to UK-based shipping market intelligence provider Clarksons Research, the benchmark newbuilding price for an LNG carrier stood at $245 million as of Oct. 23, down $3 million from $248 million in October last year. Prices for ultra-large container ships also declined over the same period, from $266.5 million to approximately $242 million. The downturn is particularly notable given that LNG carrier orders have increased more than 4.5-fold year-on-year. China’s rapid expansion in both shipbuilding capacity and technological capabilities is seen as a major factor behind the price decline. Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, previously focused on medium-sized vessels, has been securing more orders for ultra-large container ships. Hengli Heavy Industries, meanwhile, is targeting the LNG carrier market through a build-first, sell-later strategy, constructing vessels before securing buyers. Jiangnan Shipyard has also intensified price competition by securing LNG carrier orders at $225 million per vessel, undercutting prevailing benchmark prices and challenging South Korean shipbuilders’ market share. South Korean shipbuilders are unlikely to experience an immediate earnings impact, as this year’s results largely reflect vessels ordered at peak prices approximately two years ago. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering’s third-quarter operating profit is projected to rise 50.5% year-on-year to 1.5854 trillion won, while Hanwha Ocean and Samsung Heavy Industries are expected to record profit growth of 86.5% and 8.9%, respectively. However, a prolonged decline in newbuilding prices could erode profitability once their existing backlog of higher-priced orders is delivered. An oversupply of vessels and mismatches between ship deliveries and LNG project schedules are also limiting price recovery. Large numbers of vessels ordered since 2022 are entering service, while major LNG production projects, including Qatar’s North Field East, have experienced delays. With shipping capacity expanding ahead of available cargo volumes, shipowners have less incentive to pay premium prices for new vessels. Industry experts say South Korean shipbuilders need to accelerate technological development and business diversification to maintain their competitive edge over Chinese rivals. The period around 2029, when the quality and performance of vessels built by newer Chinese entrants become clearer, could prove a critical test of competitiveness. In response, Korean shipbuilders are expanding beyond conventional commercial vessels into higher-value businesses, including small modular reactor (SMR)-powered ships, offshore power generation facilities and floating liquefied natural gas production (FLNG) units. articles.body: Biofuel Bunker Snapshot: Lower feedstock costs weigh on Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 Europe Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has dropped $36/mt in the past week, even as the Dutch port’s conventional VLSFO price has gained $23/mt over the same period. This has narrowed Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $59/mt to $96/mt. Prima Markets’ ARA UCOME and POMEME barge prices, both indicators of feedstock sourcing costs, have each dropped $57/mt in the past week, to $1,625/mt and $1,695/mt respectively. Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO (POMEME) is priced at $1,360/mt, an $87/mt discount to the port’s conventional LSMGO price. B100 has been priced at $1,162/mt in Rotterdam today. Rotterdam’s B100 price has fallen by $188/mt over the past month, while its LSMGO price has risen by $77/mt. This has widened B100’s discount to LSMGO from $10/mt to $275/mt. Pricing B100 for the same energy as a tonne of LSMGO, and including EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) costs and FuelEU Maritime compliance, B100’s discount to LSMGO has widened by $222/mt to $740/mt in the same period for a ship sailing from Rotterdam to another EU port. articles.title: How Smuggling Networks Use the Same Tactics as Sanctions Evaders
articles.summary: The Problem Is the Same, So the Playbook Is the Same A vessel carrying crude loaded at a sanctioned terminal and a vessel carrying cocaine loaded off a Colombian beach are solving an identical problem. Both need to move cargo across international waters and into a port without the voyage being reconstructed...
articles.body: How Smuggling Networks Use the Same Tactics as Sanctions Evaders in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 The Problem Is the Same, So the Playbook Is the Same A vessel carrying crude loaded at a sanctioned terminal and a vessel carrying cocaine loaded off a Colombian beach are solving an identical problem. Both need to move cargo across international waters and into a port without the voyage being reconstructed afterward. The techniques that solve that problem are not commodity-specific. Going dark at the point where the record would matter. Transferring cargo at sea so the vessel entering the controlled port is not the vessel that loaded it. Changing flag, name, and MMSI so the history does not follow the hull. Declaring an origin that is not where the cargo actually came from. One Windward counter-narcotics assessment described a vessel as a textbook case of exploiting phantom registries, deliberate AIS manipulation, and corporate opacity to move illicit cargo across continents while evading detection. Every element of that sentence would be equally at home in a sanctions evasion report. The only thing that differed was what was in the hold. The compliance community and the enforcement community have historically treated these as separate problems with separate tooling. At the vessel behavior layer, they are one problem. Dark Activity Says Where, Not Why An AIS gap does not explain itself. It tells you a vessel stopped transmitting, at a particular place, for a particular duration, and then resumed. For a sanctions analyst, a vessel going dark near a designated terminal reads as an attempt to obscure a port call. For a counter-narcotics officer, a vessel going dark in open water at a known transfer area reads as an attempt to obscure a meeting. The signature is identical. A gap in the record at a location and time consistent with illicit activity, bracketed by normal transmission either side. Windward tracked a Mali-flagged general cargo vessel that left its Albanian base port in late August 2026 declaring Egypt as its destination, switched off AIS in open water off eastern Libya, and stayed dark for more than three weeks. It reappeared almost exactly where it had gone dark, immediately changed its declared destination back to Albania, and sailed straight home. Route from Albania to the dark period off eastern Libya and back, August to September 2026. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. Two details make the gap meaningful rather than ambiguous. The vessel reported normally right up to the switch-off and again immediately after reappearing, which makes a coverage failure unlikely. And it was the only vessel in the surrounding area to go dark during that period. A nine-day dark period, a first-ever call at that country lasting two hours, and a further two days lost on departure. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. A second case shows the same shape with a shorter clock. A vessel went dark for nine days, surfaced inside a bay for a two-hour call at a private wharf, and went dark again shortly after departure. The call was its first ever in that country across a 632-port-call history. Acting on that assessment, a coast guard boarded the vessel on its return leg and found empty cartons aboard, consistent with cargo already discharged. Neither case was resolved by reading the AIS record. Both were resolved by reading what the AIS record was missing, against what the vessel had done before. Transfers at Sea Serve Both Missions Ship-to-ship transfer is the single most transferable technique between the two threat profiles. Sanctioned operators use it to break the link between cargo and origin. Crude loads at a designated terminal, moves at sea to a vessel with a clean profile, and arrives at a legitimate port with documentation describing a different voyage. Trafficking networks use it for the same structural reason. Contraband moves from a vessel that cannot safely enter a controlled port to one that can, or from a mothership to a small craft that never appears in any commercial record at all. The behavior is detectable in imagery regardless of AIS status. Two hulls alongside are visible in EO and SAR whether or not either is transmitting, and draft changes consistent with a transfer are visible even when no AIS record of the event exists. The limits are worth stating honestly: A high-speed craft operating at up to 40 knots can be outside the frame by the time imagery is processed and delivered, which is why detection at the mothership end of the chain is more tractable than at the receiving end. The analytical value sits in identifying the vessel that is positioned to make the transfer, not in catching the transfer itself. Identity Changes Exist to Break the History Flag-hopping, MMSI changes, and renaming all serve one purpose across both threat profiles. They prevent a vessel’s record from following it. A hull with a documented pattern of illicit behavior reflags, renames, and reappears as a nominally clean entity. Screened on what it declares, each incarnation looks unremarkable. Screened against ownership networks and multi-year behavioral history, the underlying identity remains traceable. The flag itself is increasingly the tell. The Mali-flagged vessel above had reflagged in June 2026 following a renaming and a series of identity changes. Mali has informed the IMO that vessels are fraudulently broadcasting its flag, which means the registration cannot be read as a flag state providing oversight. The vessel did not acquire a regulator. It acquired the appearance of one. That is as relevant to a customs officer deciding whether to inspect a vessel before it berths as it is to a compliance analyst screening a counterparty. Evasion Does Not Always Mean Going Dark One case is worth including because it breaks the pattern the other examples establish. A general cargo vessel ran three consecutive voyages from Colombia to Turkey across eleven months. On each transit, it made a short stop off a stretch of Colombian coastline associated with small-craft interdictions, then roughly two weeks later slowed to under three knots on the Atlantic approach to Gibraltar before continuing into the Mediterranean toward its declared destination. AIS transmitted continuously throughout. No dark periods, no identity changes, no recorded meetings. The anomaly is not in what was hidden. It is in a slowdown with no operational purpose, repeated three times, in a location where none of nine comparable vessels slowed, on voyages that were never bound for a port near the strait. A screening model looking for concealment would return nothing here. A model assessing behavior against peer vessels and the vessel’s own history returns a question worth asking. One Architecture, Two Mission Sets Customs enforcement and sanctions compliance operate from different data systems, different alert triggers, and different evidentiary standards. The vessel behavior layer recognizes none of those distinctions. In the Caribbean, a multi-agency operation using Windward’s platform and agentic capabilities contributed to the disruption of a transnational smuggling network and the seizure of $54.5 million in illicit assets. The same behavioral models, satellite fusion, and ownership resolution underpin sanctions screening for commercial compliance teams. The practical question splits by where an agency is starting from. Agencies already using maritime intelligence for sanctions work should be asking whether their current tooling surfaces what they need for interdiction, because the behaviors overlap but the alerting usually does not. Agencies approaching maritime intelligence as a customs or counter-narcotics tool should understand that the architecture for finding the smuggling vessel is the same architecture for finding the sanctions evader. Buying one and then discovering you needed the other is a common sequence, and an avoidable one. Source: Windward 2026-11-02 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Both need to move cargo across international waters and into a port without the voyage being reconstructed afterward.
The techniques that solve that problem are not commodity-specific.
Going dark at the point where the record would matter.

articles.body: Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI) increased $46 to $1,504 per 40ft container in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 This relative stability is reflected on most lanes, indicating that, with few exceptions, carriers extended rates for the first fortnight into the second. See detailed commentary below. IACI holds steady as congestion eases • The Drewry Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI), the benchmark widely referenced by procurement teams, increased $46 to $1,504 per 40ft container. This relative stability is reflected on most lanes, indicating that, with few exceptions, carriers extended rates for the first fortnight into the second. • Spot rates from Greater China to Northeast, Southeast and South Asia were mostly stable this week. The main ports, including the large Chinese ports and the major transhipment hub Singapore, have managed to absorb the congestion, resulting in stabilisation and small reductions on Shanghai–Singapore and Shanghai–Tanjung Pelepas. Rates from Shanghai to Singapore fell 3% to $1,889 per 40ft container, while those to Tanjung Pelepas fell 2% to $2,053 per 40ft container. Some smaller ports, however, are still struggling with congestion, and rates from Shanghai to Ho Chi Minh City, Jakarta and Laem Chabang remain very high and are still rising. Jakarta is particularly sensitive because its limited operational flexibility makes it hard to cope with vessel bunching. Average vessel waiting times at Ho Chi Minh City rose from 8 to 22 hours over the past fortnight, as of Week 43. The deteriorating situation in the Middle East kept Shanghai–Jebel Ali rates elevated at $8,584 per 40ft container. Drewry expects rates to remain broadly stable in the coming weeks, although further capacity additions could add to supply and threaten market stability. • Spot rates on trade routes across Southeast and Northeast Asia remained mostly stable, except for routes originating from Jakarta and Shanghai. Rates from Jakarta to Shanghai increased 9% to $81 per 40ft container. Separately, Pacific International Lines (PIL) is set to launch its new JKS service on 5 November to strengthen its Straits–Indonesia network. The fortnightly service will deploy two vessels of 1,900–2,600 TEU, calling at Singapore, Laem Chabang and Jakarta. Drewry expects freight rates to stabilise in the coming weeks. • Geopolitical and weather-related disruption remains a key risk for Intra-Asia trade, as port closures and vessel delays could tighten capacity and put upward pressure on freight rates. Typhoon Champi, which struck East Asia on 23 October, disrupted vessel movements and caused shipping delays, while high bunker costs and ongoing US–Iran tensions continued to push rates up. The Intra-Asia container Index is already around 200% higher than a year ago. Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI) reports actual spot container freight rates for major intra-Asia trade routes. articles.body: Services Top Right Sidra Line returns to Red Sea trade with two services November 2, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Sidra Line is returning to the Red Sea trade with two container services, according to DynaLiners. The carrier will operate the Red Sea Express (RSA) between the Eastern Mediterranean and the Red Sea. It will also offer an intra-Red Sea connection under the IRS service. The RSA service will deploy one 270 TEU vessel and operate monthly. Its rotation will be: Adana – Alexandria – Sokhna – Aqaba – Djibouti – Aqaba – Damietta – Lattakia – Adana The IRS service is understood to be provided through Samsun Shipping. articles.body: The Port of Gothenburg has significantly increased yard capacity at Arken Intermodal Terminal through a reconfiguration of the railway track layout, freeing up approximately 4,000 square metres of additional yard space for trailers and other units. The result is an increase of almost double the previous yard capacity from a five percent expansion in available space. Arken Intermodal Terminal is one of Sweden’s largest intermodal terminals and a key hub for transfers between rail, road and sea. Growing cargo volumes over time had pushed capacity in certain flows close to its limit, with yard space identified as the primary constraint. The capacity improvement was achieved by rebuilding one of the through tracks at the terminal to release the additional yard area, demonstrating that smarter use of existing infrastructure can deliver substantial gains without the need for large-scale construction. Carl Johan Andersson, Senior Logistics Developer at the Port of Gothenburg, described the result as an example of capacity development through intelligent use of existing land rather than simply building bigger, noting that a five percent increase in space has delivered close to a doubling of yard capacity. Emma Meltin, Bridge Manager Intermodal at Gothenburg RoRo Terminal, highlighted the operational benefits of greater yard flexibility, enabling better flow planning, more effective peak management and reduced unnecessary cargo movements, ultimately delivering more efficient and reliable service to customers.

(U.S. Navy Photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Alice Husted) By Heidi Taksdal Skjeseth and Alberto Nardelli Oct 19, 2026 (Bloomberg) –The European Union looks to be relaxing its opposition to oil and gas production in polar areas, while still calling for all fossil fuels to be kept in the ground in its forthcoming Arctic strategy. A draft of the strategy, seen by Bloomberg, contains no references to a moratorium on new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic, marking a shift in wording from the EU’s 2021 stance . The wording has been a topic of intense discussions between the trade bloc and Norway, which has lobbied hard for the EU to abandon its climate-based opposition to oil and gas exploration in the high north. The Nordic nation awarded five oil and gas exploration licenses in the Barents Sea , which is part of the Arctic, in last year’s licensing round and opened up 38 blocks in 2026 for applications. Norway supplied almost a third of EU’s gas imports last year, including a small part from those fields. The petroleum industry’s fear was that the EU would pledge not to buy oil and gas from Norway’s new Arctic fields. Instead, the draft says the union will “prioritize” renewable energy sources and hydrocarbons produced outside the Arctic. The European Commission also says it will work toward an international commitment to prevent further development of Arctic oil and gas resources, or purchases from them, when such activity “poses a threat to the Arctic ecosystem.” In 2021, the EU had said that “building on the partial moratoriums on hydrocarbons exploration in the Arctic” in parts of the US, Canada and Greenland, “the EU is committed to ensuring that oil, coal and gas stay in the ground, including in Arctic regions” and that it would work toward “a multilateral legal obligation not to allow any further hydrocarbon reserve development in the Arctic or contiguous regions, nor to purchase such hydrocarbons if they were to be produced.” The latest draft also reiterates the EU’s broader commitment to work toward keeping coal, oil and gas in the ground, including in the Arctic, in line with its climate targets. The bloc has set a legally binding goal of cutting net greenhouse gas emissions by 90% by 2040 from the 1990 level. Related Article; Shadow Fleet Traffic on Northern Sea Route Surges as Arctic Safety Concerns Grow A spokesperson for Equinor ASA, which already produces oil and gas and is exploring more fields in the Barents Sea — referred questions to the Energy Department, and a spokesperson for the ministry declined to comment ahead of the strategy’s release. Environmental groups said the changes don’t amount to a significant retreat by Brussels. Paal Frisvold, who heads the Alliance to Preserve the Moratorium on Oil Drilling in the Arctic, told Bloomberg that he believes that the omission of the word moratorium makes the key message on climate stronger, adding “EU is determined to keep fossil fuels in the ground.” The draft text also maintains the EU’s opposition to deep-sea mining until scientific knowledge gaps have been “satisfactorily filled.” Norway in 2024 approved seabed mining , although no such works have yet started. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: By Gerry Doyle Oct 31, 2026 (Bloomberg) –As US President Donald Trump threatens renewed attacks against Iran, Tehran’s intermittent strikes on commercial vessels have left the two sides locked in a painful...

Join the leading maritime news network Smoke and fire rise from a commercial cargo vessel following a strike, which US Central Command says it had disabled in the Gulf of Oman after the ship's crew ignored warnings and attempted to run a naval blockade against Iran, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, October 10, 2026, in this still image taken from a handout video. U.S. Central Command/Handout via REUTERS By Gerry Doyle Oct 31, 2026 (Bloomberg) –As US President Donald Trump threatens renewed attacks against Iran, Tehran’s intermittent strikes on commercial vessels have left the two sides locked in a painful economic standoff. For Iran, the US blockade of its oil exports has snuffed out a key part of its military funding and severely hobbled the $300 billion economy, with only a tiny fraction of the prewar 2 million barrels per day are leaving the country via land routes. And for the US, the rising cost of shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz — even though US Central Command says almost all Iranian attacks there fail or are intercepted — has kept fuel prices high, stirring a political backlash at home with the midterm elections fast approaching. Iran doesn’t even need a high tempo of attacks to keep oil prices elevated; although shipments through the strait are at about 80% of prewar levels, the associated risk has inflated insurance costs. It was more expensive in early October to hire a supertanker in some parts of the world than it was to send a rocket into space. But even significant economic pain isn’t likely to change Iran’s ability to keep up “ harassing fire ” in the strait, said Jim Lamson, a visiting research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and former CIA analyst focused on Iran and the Middle East. A stockpile of missile components means Tehran can continue to assemble anti-ship weapons, even though US airstrikes have severely degraded its ability to manufacture them at scale, he said. “They have been planning for a long-term asymmetric conflict with the US for decades,” Lamson said. “Things like building in resilience, building in redundancy, building in stockpiling — these have been part of their military culture.” Although there have been a record of at least 28 open-source reports of damage to shipping in the strait in October, Iran has not increased its volume of attacks, according to a US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Instead, more serious damage has led to more incidents being flagged, with a quarter of the reports in the first two weeks of October involving strikes on ships’ engine rooms, which can take vessels out of service. The continued attacks by Iran leave a few options — none of them with a guaranteed favorable outcome. Trump may order the resumption of airstrikes after the election, even though these only go so far to completely shut down Iran’s ability to lob missiles into the strait — typically unsophisticated weapons that attack any ship in a target area. That leaves making the economic cost of Iranian ship attacks impossible to bear, said John Miller, a retired US Navy vice admiral and former head of CENTCOM. “As long as they want to have a blockade in place, they can continue to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz,” Miller said of Iran. “This has always been the case: You can either make them unwilling or unable.” The tanker industry is continuing to send oil out of the Middle East for now at near prewar levels, and it’s not clear what sort of escalation it would take to halt that. Transits through the waterway are earning owners of supertankers tens of millions of dollars, and the vessels’ crews several months’ pay for a few days of dangerous navigation. For now that’s proving sufficient to keep trade running. The International Maritime Organization estimates that there have been 121 incidents in Hormuz and the wider region since the war began, including 24 confirmed seafarer fatalities. Read Also: Containership Sinks as Hormuz Attacks Spiral Out of Control No ship has struck a floating min e while transiting the strait, the US official said, although Iran said as recently as late October that a mine damaged a tanker, and on Friday the UKMTO, which monitors shipping security, reported a tanker was damaged by explosives placed on its hull. Iran is using both traditional cruise missiles and drones to attack shipping, the official said, and US forces are both organizing ship transits and protecting them, largely with aircraft overhead. CENTCOM has said about 95% of ships transit the strait without incident. The US works directly with the shipping industry, sharing information and discussing timing, routes and numbers for vessels that want to pass through the strait in either direction, the US official said. US forces then formulate a plan for doing so safely, including what assets will be used to keep tabs on the journey and shoot down threats if necessary. Miller said much of Iran’s ability to track anything beyond visual range of its shores had been all but destroyed over the last eight months. As a result, the weapons it uses are often fired blind, or at the general area where Iranian strike planners think ships might be. Once the missiles arrive, radar or infrared seekers guide them to whatever is nearby. Aircraft armed with cheap munitions such as the APKWS missile, which costs about $20,000 for a BAE Systems Plc guidance kit, handle those sorts of attacks. The expensive and advanced air-defense interceptors on US Navy ships, such as the Raytheon SM-6 and SM-3 Block IIA, are then reserved for ballistic missile threats. Trump has previewed in recent days plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. But it’s not clear that airstrikes — especially against an adversary that has planned for decades to keep key capabilities safe against such attacks — will change the situation in the strait, said Emma Salisbury, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and an associate fellow at the Royal Navy Strategic Studies Centre. A surge in fighting could push oil prices into the $120-$130 range, according to analysis by Bloomberg Economics chief emerging markets economist Ziad Daoud. Both sides “may prefer a brief conflict to improve their negotiating power,” he wrote. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Ann Wang TAIPEI, Nov 1 (Reuters) – China’s Coast Guard is harassing shipping with its latest patrol off Taiwan’s east coast and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction, the Taiwanese Coast Guard said, adding it had sent its own ships to keep watch. China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing’s sovereignty ?claims, say they believe China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets. Taipei regards the area off its east ?coast as critical to wartime supply routes from allies in the event of a blockade or conflict. China recognizes no claims of sovereignty by Taiwan. Responding late Saturday to China’s announcement of its latest east coast patrol, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said two Chinese ships were involved and it had sent its own forces to monitor. Chinese state media showed video of one of its ships broadcasting a radio message that it was carrying out law enforcement and offering help should any be needed. It did not say who the message was broadcast at, but showed footage of an unidentified fishing trawler. Taiwan’s Coast Guard said China’s “attempts to harass ships at sea through radio communications are a clear expansion of power that violate international law, undermine regional peace and stability, and deviate from reality.” “Our country holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan, and China has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan’s waters,” it added. China on Saturday also sent another Coast Guard ship close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands, which are strategically located at the top of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said separately. Taiwan has so far this year “expelled” Chinese Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times, it added. The Pratas have no permanent civilian population and lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong. In its latest statement, the IRGC Navy said a fourth vessel, a tanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, had hit a mine, suffered a powerful explosion and was burning. An IRGC Navy statement had said earlier that one of the tankers, which was also carrying 2 million barrels of crude oil, had hit a naval mine. Reuters was unable to immediately verify the statement. Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said it had received a report of an incident in the Strait of Hormuz. A potential strike threatening operations at some of the busiest container terminals in the United States has been pushed back after the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) and the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 agreed to extend negotiations through November 4. PMA announced Friday that the two sides had signed an extension through 5 p.m. Pacific Time on Wednesday, November 4, avoiding a potential walkout that had been threatened for November 1. Negotiations will continue with assistance from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. The dispute involves approximately 250 maritime watchmen represented by ILWU Local 26 who perform security-related duties at terminals throughout the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Despite the relatively small number of workers involved, the potential disruption is significant. According to PMA, Local 26 members work at terminals handling roughly 85% of cargo moving through the Port of Long Beach and 33% at the Port of Los Angeles. As gCaptain previously reported , a strike could have consequences well beyond the watchmen themselves. PMA has warned that other ILWU workers are unlikely to cross Local 26 picket lines, potentially halting vessel, yard and gate operations at affected terminals. The union had identified eight terminal locations that could be affected by a walkout. The two sides have been negotiating a new agreement since the previous contract expired in July 2025. Local 26 has accused employers of failing to make meaningful progress, while PMA has maintained that significant differences remain despite more than a year of bargaining. “PMA remains committed to reaching a fair agreement at the bargaining table that avoids disruption at the nation’s two busiest ports,” the employer association said Friday. The extension provides several additional days for negotiators to reach an agreement, but the underlying labor dispute remains unresolved. The stakes are particularly high for the Southern California port complex, which handled a combined record 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in September. For now, the immediate strike threat has been postponed, with the next deadline set for Wednesday afternoon. articles.title: How MARAD Cut Years Off Deepwater Port Reviews Without Changing Environmental Standards
articles.summary: As gCaptain reported earlier this week, the Maritime Administration (MARAD) announced its approval of the $8.2 billion Texas ST LNG export port application, a major development for U.S. energy production. But the announcement also highlighted another significant milestone: the fastest deepwater port license review in...

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Wojciech Wrzesien / Shutterstock By Tom Ewing (gCaptain) – As gCaptain reported earlier this week , the Maritime Administration (MARAD) announced its approval of the $8.2 billion Texas ST LNG export port application, a major development for U.S. energy production. But the announcement also highlighted another significant milestone: the fastest deepwater port license review in more than 20 years. According to the Department of Transportation (DOT) , the review was completed nearly 3.7 years faster than the historical average, representing a 70% reduction in review time. The acceleration follows changes implemented in January, when MARAD assumed the lead role in deepwater port reviews and the U.S. Coast Guard shifted to a supporting role focused on vessel operations, maritime safety and security. ST LNG filed its application with MARAD and the Coast Guard on June 9, 2025. Under the streamlined approach, MARAD completed the Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) in just 410 days. DOT credited the changes with eliminating unnecessary administrative procedures and accelerating the review process. In response to DOT’s announcement, gCaptain followed up with questions seeking additional insight into which specific changes had the greatest impact on reducing red tape. A DOT spokesperson, speaking on background, said “the primary efficiency gained was fixing a structural inefficiency, rather than addressing challenges within any specific partner agency.” Previously, MARAD and the U.S. Coast Guard operated under a co-lead structure for reviews required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). DOT’s spokesperson said this shared responsibility for environmental reviews “inadvertently created duplicative administrative steps, parallel document routing, and sequential reviews.” Now, with MARAD serving as the sole lead agency, project schedules have been consolidated and the review team has established a unified approach to interagency communication. “The U.S. Coast Guard remains an important partner in this process,” DOT explained, adding that “this shift simply allows them to focus purely on their core statutory missions of maritime safety, security, and operational risk assessment, while MARAD drives the environmental timeline.” The Coast Guard is listed in the project’s Record of Decision (ROD) as one of six federal cooperating agencies, but the document does not otherwise include or reference specific Coast Guard statements. Neither U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 6 nor the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, two other federal partners, filed objections or concerns regarding application approval. The deepwater port development will consist of four phases. Each phase includes five fixed offshore platforms (Gas Treatment, Liquefaction, Bridge Support Trestle, LNG Transfer, and Accommodation and Utilities), bridges linking the platforms, a dolphin mooring system composed of three berthing dolphins and six mooring dolphins, and a moored LNG Floating Storage Unit (FSU). At full build-out, the deepwater port will include 20 platforms, four FSUs, four mooring systems, and 7.7 miles of pipeline, consisting of a 5.6-mile lateral pipeline and 2.1 miles of interconnecting pipelines between the phases. DOT was asked whether the ST LNG project benefited from any one-time procedural exemptions that might not apply to future projects. DOT’s answer: No. Going forward, MARAD’s leadership role and the related procedural steps will follow the changes formally established in January. DOT was also asked to identify the types of red tape that have historically impeded timely reviews, such as repetitive filings or demands for unnecessary information. The spokesperson said the primary efficiency came from eliminating duplicative administrative procedures. Under the previous co-lead model, draft environmental documents, requests for information and legal reviews often had to move sequentially between multiple agencies before they could advance or be published. “By consolidating the NEPA (National Environmental Policy Act) process under MARAD,” DOT said, “we established a single Federal docket and a unified project management team. We eliminated redundant legal and administrative processing, aligned our public comment periods, and streamlined how cooperating agencies provide input.” Finally, DOT was asked about environmental reviews that must proceed according to nature’s timetable, such as studies involving temperature cycles, migration patterns or other seasonal factors. Were there opportunities to streamline reviews of environmental processes that inherently take weeks or months to evaluate? DOT replied: “Streamlining our administrative process does not mean cutting corners on rigorous environmental science or biological mandates.” To manage extended seasonal or biological studies efficiently, the spokesperson said MARAD is “front-loading” interagency coordination. MARAD’s team is engaging cooperating agencies, such as NOAA Fisheries, earlier in the scoping and pre-application phases to identify required biological studies as soon as possible. MARAD is also seeking to maximize the use of existing regional data from prior offshore projects to satisfy baseline requirements where appropriate, reducing the need for duplicative studies conducted from scratch. DOT noted that “when project-specific seasonal data collection is legally required, we integrate those study schedules into a predictable, concurrent review timeline rather than letting them cause cascading, sequential delays. This approach ensures we maintain the exact same statutory level of environmental assurance while drastically reducing idle administrative time in the schedule.” To be clear, MARAD’s application approval is not the same as the issuance of a license to operate. In fact, MARAD’s approval is conditional. ST LNG must agree in writing not to make changes to its deepwater port application and must demonstrate compliance with nine conditions before a license can be issued. Those conditions cover matters ranging from financial responsibility and oil spill liability to eventual decommissioning. The required compliance documentation must be submitted at least 90 days before a license can be issued. articles.summary: Hanwha Philly Shipyard has secured a $269 million contract to build a Medium Landing Ship (LSM) for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, marking a major milestone in the South...

Join the leading maritime news network Artist’s rendering of the U.S. Navy’s planned Medium Landing Ship (LSM), designed to transport Marines, equipment and supplies in support of expeditionary operations. (Image: U.S. Navy) Hanwha Philly Shipyard has secured a $269 million contract to build a Medium Landing Ship (LSM) for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, marking a major milestone in the South Korean company’s push into U.S. naval shipbuilding. TOTE Services announced Friday that it selected Hanwha Defense USA (HDUSA) as the first shipbuilder under its $2.2 billion Vessel Construction Manager (VCM) contract for the LSM program. The award covers construction of one vessel at the Philadelphia shipyard, with options for three additional ships. Construction is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027, with the program’s first vessel scheduled for delivery in 2030. The selection follows a competitive bidding process launched in July and comes just days after Hanwha announced plans to place its Philadelphia shipyard under the control of its U.S. defense subsidiary. “Since acquiring Philly Shipyard in 2024, Hanwha has made significant investments in its workforce and technology to pave the way to build ships for the U.S. Navy and other federal customers,” said HDUSA President and CEO Michael Coulter. The contract represents Hanwha Defense USA’s first U.S. Navy shipbuilding award and a significant step in the company’s effort to transform the former commercial shipyard into a dual-use facility serving both military and commercial customers. TOTE Services said Hanwha was selected based on its competitive pricing and acceptance of subcontract terms and conditions. The company is also continuing contract discussions with Bollinger Shipyards and Fincantieri Marinette Marine, which are expected to participate in construction of the LSM fleet. “This award shows the speed at which the VCM model can move from RFP to contract,” said TOTE Services President Jeff Dixon. “Through a competitive process, we secured strong terms that benefit the government, along with build positions that allow construction to start in the fourth quarter of 2027.” The LSM program is intended to provide the Marine Corps with smaller amphibious vessels capable of transporting personnel, equipment and supplies between islands and coastal locations, particularly in the Indo-Pacific. The Navy and Marine Corps are planning a fleet of 35 vessels, with TOTE’s initial contract covering up to eight ships. The award also builds on an existing relationship between TOTE Services and the Philadelphia yard. Under a separate VCM arrangement with the U.S. Maritime Administration, TOTE has overseen construction of the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel (NSMV) program at Philly Shipyard. Four of the five training ships have already been delivered. “Hanwha Philly Shipyard has already built and delivered four National Security Multi-Mission Vessels under the VCM model with TOTE Services, and we will leverage that experience to deliver the LSM to the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps,” said Tim Glinatsis, senior vice president of program management at HDUSA. The announcement comes amid a broader restructuring of Hanwha’s U.S. shipbuilding operations. As gCaptain recently reported , Hanwha Defense USA announced this week that it is acquiring a controlling stake in Hanwha Philly Shipyard, shifting the facility toward defense-led ownership as the company expands its U.S. naval shipbuilding business. Hanwha acquired the shipyard in December 2024 and has since been investing in workforce development, infrastructure and technology to support an expansion into naval construction. The shift has also raised questions about the future balance between military and commercial shipbuilding at one of the country’s major Jones Act shipyards. Asked by gCaptain whether Hanwha would maintain and expand commercial Jones Act shipbuilding capacity as the yard transitions toward defense-led ownership, a company spokesperson said it was “in a good position to compete and build for commercial and naval demand as a dual-use yard.” Friday’s contract announcement provides the clearest indication yet of how Hanwha intends to put that strategy into practice, establishing a foothold in Navy ship construction while positioning the Philadelphia facility to compete for additional government and commercial work. October 30, 2026 Bureau Veritas launches Cruise Center of Excellence at Cruise Lines International Association Cruise Forward Summit 2026. © BV Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore (BV) has announced the launch of a new Cruise Center of Excellence in Miami, to connect customers in local proximity to a global network of BV experts dedicated to supporting operators as they navigate increasingly complex market environments. The cruise hub joins BV’s global network of Centers of Excellence across sectors including Gas (Doha) and Offshore (Singapore, Shanghai, and Kuala Lumpur). With the launch of the dedicated Cruise Center of Excellence, BV is well positioned to support clients in turning ambitious concepts into viable designs, as well as helping operators to navigate evolving market requirements whilst improving performance throughout the life of their assets. BV has experience within the cruise sector and supports some of the largest cruise operators across a broad range of specialisms. Its expertise spans decarbonization strategies, from wind propulsion to bio-LNG capability for large cruise ships, alongside industry-leading advisory services covering fire safety, lifeboat arrangements, evacuation analysis, and smoke and fire propagation simulations. The Center also provides expertise in emerging technologies, digitalization and cybersecurity to support future-ready cruise operations. Recent examples of BV’s capabilities within the Cruise sector range from providing dedicated monitoring and validation support to MSC Cruises to secure independent verification and Flag State recognition of actual methane emissions from its vessels, MSC World Europa and MSC Euribia, to support FuelEU Maritime compliance. Furthermore, BV has partnered with Brittany Ferries and Adrena to demonstrate fuel savings of up to 6% through the deployment of an advanced digital twin-enabled routing solution In addition, BV is at the forefront of advancing wind propulsion technologies and enabling their adoption across the maritime sector. Recently, BV provided classification services to support the delivery of the 220-meter Orient Express Corinthian, which represents the world’s largest sailing cruise ship. articles.summary: StormGeo, part of Alfa Laval, has acquired Portchain, a provider of berth alignment software connecting terminals and carriers through shared, real-time port call data. The acquisition adds port call coordination to StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence…
articles.body: Portchain Acquired by StormGeo, Advancing Just-in-Time Voyage Optimization Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 Just-In Time port call coordination with Portchain. © Portchain/StormGeo StormGeo, part of Alfa Laval, has acquired Portchain, a provider of berth alignment software connecting terminals and carriers through shared, real-time port call data. The acquisition adds port call coordination to StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence, creating the foundation for a new approach to Just-in-Time voyage optimization at scale. The goal is to connect decisions about route and speed with the latest information on berth availability and terminal plans, helping operators respond to changes while a vessel is still at sea. Portchain connects container carriers and terminals through shared operational data. Portchain Connect supports digital alignment of vessel schedules and cargo volumes, while Portchain Quay supports berth, crane and workforce planning in a shared, real-time environment. Today, the Portchain Network connects shipping lines with more than 200 terminals, representing over 40% of global container terminal capacity. StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence combines voyage optimization, vessel-performance insight and expert route guidance to help operators optimize for arrival time, fuel consumption or the balance between the two. Portchain adds a shared, real-time view of berth plans aligned with terminal operators and their resources. As the companies develop this combined offering, a change in the expected berth time could inform speed decisions while the vessel is still at sea. Operators could reassess the voyage plan and better align the vessel’s estimated time of arrival (ETA) with its estimated time of berthing (ETB). Updated arrival information will also help terminals plan berths, cranes and teams. This is the foundation for Just-in-Time voyage optimization at scale: turning a change in the terminal plan into a timely voyage decision. The aim is to help vessels arrive closer to when the terminal is ready to receive them, reducing avoidable waiting, fuel use and emissions while making arrivals more predictable. The acquisition advances StormGeo’s ambition to connect weather, vessel and port insights in support of more efficient and predictable maritime operations. Together with Alfa Laval’s marine portfolio, it supports customers’ efforts to improve operational efficiency and progress towards decarbonization. The addition also strengthens Alfa Laval’s offering across the fuel transition and energy efficiency by adding StormGeo’s expertise in routing and port call coordination, with digitalization and AI helping to simplify maritime operations. Portchain will operate as an independent company under StormGeo for the next few years and will later be fully integrated into StormGeo’s portfolio. Existing Portchain customers will see no disruption to their service, and the combined offering will be available through StormGeo.
